record.original_question: Fix an integer k > 0. Are there only finitely many quadruples of integers p, q, x, y, all greater than 1, satisfying the exponential Diophantine equation x^p - y^q = k?

evidence.quote: Let k > 0 be an integer. There is only a finite number of solutions in integers p, q, x, y, each greater than 1, to the equation x^p - y^q = k.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be a fixed positive integer. Consider the exponential Diophantine equation
$$x^p - y^q = k$$
in unknowns $p, q, x, y$, where each of $p, q, x, y$ is an integer greater than $1$. Prove or disprove: for every such fixed $k$, the equation has only finitely many solutions $(p, q, x, y)$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is Pillai's conjecture (1931/1936). It remains an open problem in general; it is known to follow from the abc conjecture, and various special cases have been settled, but no unconditional proof of the full statement is known.

status_evidence.title: Pillai's Conjecture -- Wolfram MathWorld
status_evidence.snippet: Pillai's conjecture states that for fixed positive integers A, B, C the equation Ax^n - By^m = C has only finitely many solutions...
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture in its general form is stated as still a conjecture.

status_evidence.title: Perfect Powers: Pillai's works and their developments (Waldschmidt)
status_evidence.snippet: Pillai's conjecture remains open; it would follow from the abc conjecture.
status_evidence.claim: Pillai's conjecture is still open in general and would follow from abc.
